faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Titusville?
faqs.a: Pricing in Titusville hinges on what we find in the attic: a single raccoon entering through one broken soffit is a short job, while a roof-rat colony spread through wall voids with several palm-to-roof bridges takes longer and needs more sealing. We walk the roof and attic first, photograph every opening, and hand you a written figure before a trap is set — nothing is quoted blind from the driveway.

faqs.q: A snake showed up by my Titusville seawall — is it dangerous?
faqs.a: Most snakes along the lagoon are harmless black racers or ratsnakes, but the cottonmouth is a genuine Titusville resident around swales, seawalls, and dock pilings, so we never ask you to guess. Send a photo from a safe distance and we will identify it. The venomous list this far south is short — cottonmouth, eastern diamondback, dusky pygmy rattlesnake, and coralsnake — and a big docile black snake could be a protected eastern indigo, which is left alone and reported, never handled as a removal job.

Titusville.wildlife_intro:
Titusville sits squeezed between the Indian River Lagoon and the refuge lands around the space center, and that edge-of-the-wild layout shapes our work here. Raccoons den in chimneys of the older riverfront blocks and raid dumpsters behind the downtown shops, while roof rats commute along palm crowns and power lines into the attics of garden-style subdivisions. Armadillos root up irrigated lawns overnight and eastern moles ridge the sandy yards, and after summer storms cottonmouths turn up along lagoon seawalls and drainage swales.

Work here runs twelve months a year. When bats settle in a tile roofline we plan the one-way exclusion for the legal window, August 15 through April 15, because sealing a maternity colony between April 16 and August 14 is prohibited in Florida. Every job starts with your authorization under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 — the state issues no trapper license — and ends with the entry points closed so the problem stays solved.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Melbourne?
faqs.a: In Melbourne the quote follows the roof. Tile work is slower than shingle because each valley and ridge opening has to be sealed without cracking tiles, and a bat colony in a tile roof adds guano cleanup on top of exclusion. We inspect, count the openings, check the attic for droppings and chewed wiring, and give you one written number covering removal, sealing, and cleanup before we begin.

faqs.q: Can bats be removed from my Melbourne tile roof in June?
faqs.a: Not by exclusion — June sits inside Florida's bat maternity season, April 16 through August 14, when blocking or excluding bats from a roost is prohibited. What we can do in June is inspect, confirm the species — usually Brazilian free-tailed or evening bats here — seal every opening except the active exits, and schedule the one-way exclusion for after August 15, when it is legal again through April 15. If a bat turns up inside living space, keep people and pets out of the room and call us the same day.

Melbourne.wildlife_intro:
Melbourne sprawls from the Eau Gallie arts district and the Indian River bluffs out to master-planned streets in Viera and Suntree, and the calls change with the zip code. In the older river neighborhoods it is Brazilian free-tailed bats in barrel-tile roofs and raccoons in chimneys; out west, armadillos tear up new sod, moles tunnel the sandy lots, and opossums move into crawl spaces under raised older homes. Roof rats are the constant everywhere — citrus, palms, and bird feeders keep them fed year-round.

Because so many Melbourne roofs are tile, our inspections start with the valleys, ridge caps, and plumbing stacks where rats and squirrels chew through. Gray squirrels are the only squirrels we handle — fox squirrels may not be taken in Florida — and any live trap we set is checked within 24 hours as state rule requires. Call (844) 544-3498 and describe what you are hearing overhead; scratching at dawn usually means squirrels, while heavy thumps after dark point to raccoons.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Palm Bay?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the home needs afterward. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: Why are roof rats such a problem in Palm Bay?
faqs.a: Roof rats are Florida's main structure rat, and Palm Bay gives them exactly what they want: palm crowns, fruit trees, dense shrubs, and rooflines they can reach from fences and branches. They nest in attics and wall voids and breed year-round here. Our crew traps and excludes — sealing the entry and cutting back roof access — and frames structure work as nonchemical trapping and exclusion, because chemical rodent work in a structure is FDACS Chapter 482 pest-control territory.

faqs.q: There is a big burrow at the edge of our Palm Bay yard. Is it an armadillo or a gopher tortoise?
faqs.a: The shape usually tells: a gopher tortoise burrow is a wide half-moon, as broad as the tortoise is long, with a fan of sand in front — and it is protected by Florida law, so it cannot be dug, filled, or disturbed, and the tortoise cannot be removed. An armadillo burrow is rounder and steeper, more like a drilled hole. Send us a photo or have us look on a visit; the identification matters because the legal answer is opposite. If it is an armadillo burrow, we trap the resident and backfill and screen the opening; if it is a tortoise burrow, we leave it entirely alone and solve any other wildlife problem around it.

faqs.q: We keep seeing snakes near our home by the Compound. Should we be worried?
faqs.a: Worth a call, not a panic. Most snakes on Palm Bay's scrub edges are black racers and rat snakes — nonvenomous, and genuinely useful. The one to respect is the dusky pygmy rattlesnake, small, thick-bodied, and common in palmetto scrub; it is a leave-it-alone-and-call animal, especially with kids or dogs using the yard. We will identify what you are seeing from a photo or on site, remove a venomous snake that has taken up at the house itself, and tell you plainly when the right answer is to let a harmless one keep hunting your fence line.

Palm Bay.wildlife_intro:
In Palm Bay, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — long coastal Space Coast suburbs, lagoon and river frontage, and refuge land — and features such as Indian River Lagoon, Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, St. Johns River, Banana River keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Palm Bay jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

Palm Bay is the biggest city in Brevard County by land and by sprawl — tens of thousands of homes spread across a grid carved from pine flatwoods, and a huge share of our county's wildlife work happens inside that grid. The flatwoods never actually left: between the subdivisions stand vacant wooded lots, drainage canals, and the Turkey Creek corridor, so raccoons, armadillos, and eastern moles are not visitors here, they are neighbours. Armadillos dig the sandy lawns and get under slabs across the whole city; moles run the same sand; raccoons take the attics of the older sections and the chimneys everywhere; and the canal banks hold more wildlife per mile than any fence line in the county.

Palm Bay also has the Compound — the vast, unfinished street grid in the southwest where roads were paved for a city that has not arrived yet. Around its edges, homes back onto open scrub, and the animal pressure reflects it: this is where the snake calls concentrate, where raccoons commute from deep cover, and where a homeowner learns that a vacant lot in Florida is a wildlife property with no house on it yet. Our Palm Bay inspections weight the lot lines and the canal banks as heavily as the roofline, because here the habitat is not behind the neighbourhood — it is woven through it.
Palm Bay.extendedBody:
Gopher tortoises: the neighbour you work around

Palm Bay's sandy uplands are gopher tortoise country, and their burrows — wide, half-moon openings with a sand apron — are all over the vacant lots and the edges of the older subdivisions. Gopher tortoises are a protected species in Florida: their burrows cannot be disturbed, and we do not remove them. What we do is tell you honestly when the burrow on your lot line is a tortoise's, because everything else changes with that identification — armadillo burrows are narrower and steeper, and confusing the two leads people to exactly the wrong response. Other animals use abandoned tortoise burrows too, so a tortoise address can still have a wildlife problem; it just gets solved around the burrow, never through it.

The grid, the canals, and the standard Palm Bay roofline

Most Palm Bay housing is slab-on-grade suburbia from the 1980s forward, and its entries are the standard set, made worse by sand and storms: soffit vents with rusted screens, gable vents, garage-door corners, and the gaps where lanai roofs meet the house. Raccoons and gray squirrels use the roofline; roof rats use the palms the landscaping planted against it; armadillos and moles work below. Our work runs under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — and a full Palm Bay job normally touches both levels: the animals out, the roofline sealed, and the burrow openings at the slab backfilled and screened.

Snakes in the scrub edges

The scrub and flatwoods edges — around the Compound, along Turkey Creek, on any lot backing to vacant land — produce Palm Bay's snake calls: racers and rat snakes most often, pygmy rattlesnakes in the palmettos more often than people expect. We identify what is actually there before anything else. Most yard snakes here are nonvenomous and best left alone, and we will say so; a venomous snake established at a house, or any snake inside the structure, is a removal call, handled by people who do it weekly.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Cocoa?
faqs.a: Cocoa quotes turn on access and construction. A block ranch with one chewed vent is quick; a converted carport or an addition with layered rooflines can hide three or four entries that each need sealing. We inspect the whole roofline rather than guessing from the one hole you spotted, then price removal and exclusion together in writing so there are no add-ons mid-job.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Cocoa yard at night — what is it?
faqs.a: Conical holes a few inches deep scattered across the lawn almost always mean a nine-banded armadillo hunting grubs, while a raised ridge you can press down with your foot is an eastern mole tunnel, and a fan of loose sand can be a southeastern pocket gopher mound. One caution: a large half-moon burrow with a wide sandy apron is a gopher tortoise burrow — that animal is State Threatened, the burrow gets a 25-foot hands-off buffer, and it is a referral, not a digging job. Armadillos, by contrast, are lawful removal work here, and a trapped armadillo can be released on site or within Brevard County on 40-plus acres with written landowner permission.

Cocoa.wildlife_intro:
Cocoa mixes a working riverfront village, older block neighborhoods along the US-1 corridor, and the fast-growing subdivisions pushing west toward the St. Johns. Our staple call is the roof rat: mango, citrus, and dense palms around Cocoa Village feed colonies that move into attics through overhanging branches. Raccoons follow the river and the canal banks, armadillos work the sandy yards, and in the older in-town blocks, opossums and feral cats stir up most of the nighttime noise complaints that turn out not to be raccoons at all.

We handle Cocoa jobs the Florida way — trapping and exclusion on the ground, with structure rat work kept nonchemical, because pesticide-based rodent control belongs to FDACS Chapter 482 pest control licensing, a different credential from wildlife work under Rule 68A-9.010. After removal we trim-back recommendations and metal flashing on the entry holes matter more than any trap count, especially on the older bungalows where fascia has gone soft.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Merritt Island?
faqs.a: On Merritt Island, waterfront construction drives the figure. Sealing a canal home can mean working over water, screening dock and seawall gaps, and repairing pool-cage doors that raccoons have learned to lift. We scope all of that in the inspection, separate the must-do entries from the cosmetic ones, and put the full removal-and-sealing price in writing before starting.

faqs.q: Do you relocate raccoons from Merritt Island?
faqs.a: Only inside the lines Florida law draws. A live-captured native raccoon must be released on your own property, or released within Brevard County on at least 40 contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission in hand, and it all has to happen within 24 hours — and never during a county rabies alert. In practice, on a canal lot the lasting answer is exclusion: remove the animal, then seal the roofline so the next raccoon finds no way in. That is the approach we recommend for island homes.

Merritt Island.wildlife_intro:
Merritt Island is exactly that — an island, pinched between the Banana River and the Indian River, laced with residential canals, and bordered by refuge land at its north end. Water on every side means raccoons travel seawalls and dock lines, roof rats nest in sailboat-adjacent palms and attic insulation, and opossums den under waterfront decks. The canal neighborhoods also produce our most delicate calls: manatee-era seawall lots where a burrow under a patio has to be identified before anyone digs.

Because the island's housing sits so close to refuge habitat, exclusion quality is everything — a poorly sealed Merritt Island attic is reoccupied within weeks. We use chew-proof materials on soffit and roof returns, check traps daily, and release native animals only where Florida rule allows: on your property, or inside the county on 40 or more contiguous acres with written permission, within 24 hours of capture. Bats in a waterfront roof get the same seasonal respect as everywhere in Florida — exclusion only from August 15 to April 15.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Satellite Beach?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the home needs afterward. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins, with no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: I found a big snake in my Satellite Beach yard — what kind is it likely to be?
faqs.a: Most Florida snakes are nonvenomous and beneficial, and identification comes first. The venomous snakes in most of Florida are the cottonmouth, eastern diamondback rattlesnake, dusky pygmy rattlesnake, and harlequin coralsnake. A large, docile black snake may be an eastern indigo snake, which is federally Threatened — leave it alone, photograph it from a distance, and call FWC. Never handle a snake you cannot identify, and call us for an identification before anyone tries to move it.

faqs.q: Raccoons are denning under our Satellite Beach dock and getting on the roof. How do you handle the water side?
faqs.a: As part of the house, because the raccoons do. We remove the animals from the dock and deck voids, screen those voids so the under-deck space stops being a den, and seal the roofline entries they reach from the seawall and palms — plus map the palm fronds bridging to the roof for trimming. Sealing only the roof leaves the den under the dock intact, and a den that close re-tests the roofline nightly until it finds the one gap somebody missed. Doing both ends in one job is what ends it.

faqs.q: We found bat droppings along the fascia in May. What happens next?
faqs.a: A confirmation visit first — the staining and guano pattern tells us the colony's size and entries — and then honest scheduling: Florida law prohibits excluding bats during the maternity season, April 16 through August 14, because the pups cannot fly. So a May colony is mapped in May and excluded when the window opens August 15, with one-way devices at the active entries and every secondary gap sealed, in materials chosen for salt air. If a bat turns up inside the living space before then, call the same day; a single indoor bat is handled immediately, whatever the calendar says.

Satellite Beach is a barrier-island city, a mile of land between the Banana River and the Atlantic, and everything about its wildlife work is compressed by that geography. The canal-front homes off the river side put raccoons and roof rats in the palms and on the rooflines within feet of the water; the ocean side adds the dune and sea-grape edges; and the whole city is close enough that an animal's territory spans both shores. Brazilian free-tailed bats work the fascia gaps of the older beach homes, opossums den under the raised decks, and armadillos dig the sandy yards from the river to A1A — there is no part of Satellite Beach that is not waterfront-adjacent habitat.

Patrick Space Force Base fences the city's south, and the base's open land holds a standing wildlife population that commutes the fence line into the southern neighbourhoods. Add the canal system — a raccoon in Satellite Beach travels by water and seawall as much as by land — and our inspections here always walk the lot's water side as carefully as its roof: seawall burrows, dock structures, and the deck voids are part of the same address the animals are using.
Satellite Beach.extendedBody:
Canal-front work: the seawall is part of the house

On Satellite Beach's canals, a home's wildlife defences start at the water. Raccoons den under docks and in the voids beneath canal-side decks, climb from the seawall to the roofline where palms overhang, and treat the canal system as a private road network that never has traffic. We inspect and seal accordingly: deck and dock voids screened, the palm bridges to the roof mapped for trimming, roofline entries closed in metal that tolerates salt air — beach-side hardware corrodes, and a seal that rusts out in two seasons is a subscription, not a fix. Roof rats ride the same canal canopy, and their jobs combine the trapping with the full bridge-and-entry audit.

Bats, the base fence line, and the rules in Florida

Free-tailed bat colonies in the older beach homes are the city's other constant — small fascia gaps, big colonies, and a strict legal calendar. Florida allows bat exclusion only from August 15 through April 15; during the April 16 to August 14 maternity season, blocking bats is illegal. Colonies found in spring are mapped and scheduled, then excluded completely when the window opens. All of our work is done under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization; Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license. Along the Patrick fence line, we will also give you the straight answer on what the base's open land means for your street: a standing population next door is a reason to seal thoroughly once, not a reason for repeat trapping forever.

Salt air and the sealing standard

Barrier-island sealing has to be specified for the environment: galvanised and stainless materials, fasteners that will not streak or fail, and screen work that survives storm season. A Satellite Beach job is inspected with the hurricane question in mind too — loose soffits and tired fascia are both wildlife entries in October and wind failures in a storm, and closing them properly serves the house twice.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Rockledge?
faqs.a: Rockledge pricing usually comes down to canopy and roof age. Houses under heavy oaks need branch-bridge entries sealed at several points, and older shingles can mean replacing a section of rotted decking before flashing will hold. We document each entry with photos during inspection, then quote the complete job — animals out, holes sealed, attic checked — as one written figure.

faqs.q: Are the snakes in my Rockledge yard venomous?
faqs.a: Usually not. The snake we identify most often here is the southern black racer — fast, thin, and harmless — followed by eastern ratsnakes around sheds and woodpiles. Venomous possibilities in this part of Brevard are the cottonmouth near ponds and canals, the small dusky pygmy rattlesnake in palmetto and mulch edges, the eastern diamondback in scrubby lots, and the shy coralsnake. Photograph any snake from a distance rather than approaching it; we will confirm the species, and protected species such as the eastern indigo are referred, never removed.

Rockledge.wildlife_intro:
Rockledge, Brevard's oldest city, layers historic riverfront streets over postwar subdivisions and the big planned communities around Viera's western edge. Live oaks draped over the older blocks drop acorns that feed gray squirrels straight onto shingle roofs, and the Fiske Boulevard corridor's mature landscaping keeps roof rats supplied year-round. Farther west, newer streets back onto retention ponds and scrub where armadillos dig, pygmy rattlesnakes occasionally surface in palmetto edges, and sandhill cranes — protected, and strictly look-don't-touch — stroll the fairway-style lawns.

Our Rockledge inspections pay special attention to oak-to-roof contact and to the tile transitions on newer homes. If the digging in your yard turns out to be a gopher tortoise burrow, we stop, explain the 25-foot buffer, and point you to the FWC tortoise program; if it is armadillo or mole work, we handle it directly under your authorization. Either way you get a straight identification before any quote is written.
